blocks.heading: 💪 BP Formula
blocks.html:
BP = Cardiac Output x Peripheral Vascular Resistance

CO = Heart Rate x Stroke Volume
Normal BP Regulation

blocks.heading: ✅ Normal Values
blocks.html:
Normal BP: <120/80 mmHg

Elevated: 120-129 / <80 mmHg

Stage 1 HTN: 130-139 / 80-89 mmHg

Stage 2 HTN: ≥140 / ≥90 mmHg
Baroreceptors detect BP changes
Brain adjusts HR & vessel tone

blocks.heading: 💡 What the Nurse Must Know
blocks.html:
• Heart pumps blood through arteries to deliver O₂ to tissues
  • Baroreceptors in carotid sinus & aortic arch regulate BP
  • RAAS: Kidneys release renin to control BP
  • Blood vessels vasodilate and vasoconstrict
RAAS regulates long-term BP control
Normal BP Maintained: <120/80

blocks.heading: NORMAL FUNCTION
blocks.html:
• Blood vessels are relaxed
  • Blood flows freely to all tissues
  • BP stays within normal range
  • Heart pumps at normal workload
  • Baroreceptors maintain homeostasis

blocks.heading: DYSFUNCTION
blocks.html:
• Chronic vasoconstriction
  • Increased vascular resistance
  • Heart must pump harder
  • Endothelial damage occurs
  • Baroreceptors reset to higher BP

blocks.heading: ⚠ Risk Factors (Non-Modifiable)
blocks.html:
• Family history of hypertension
  • Age >55 years
  • African Caribbean ethnicity
  • Male gender (until menopause)
  • Chronic kidney disease

blocks.heading: 💡 Risk Factors (Modifiable)
blocks.html:
• Obesity / high sodium intake
  • Physical inactivity
  • Smoking / excess alcohol
  • Diabetes / high cholesterol
  • Chronic stress

blocks.heading: 🔥 Uncontrolled HTN Leads To:
blocks.html:
Heart Failure • Stroke • Myocardial Infarction • CKD • Vision Loss • Aortic Aneurysm

NRG Opposite: High pressure damages vessel walls → atherosclerosis → organ damage

blocks.heading: ⚡ RAAS Cascade Detail
blocks.html:
Renin (from kidneys) converts angiotensinogen → Angiotensin I

ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) converts ATI → Angiotensin II

Angiotensin II causes:

  • Potent vasoconstriction (raises BP directly)
  • Aldosterone release (Na⁺/H₂O retention)
  • ADH release (further fluid retention)

blocks.heading: 🎯 Result: Sustained Hypertension
blocks.html:
• Increased blood volume (Na⁺/H₂O retention)
  • Chronic vasoconstriction → sustained high BP
  • Endothelial damage → atherosclerosis
  • Left ventricular hypertrophy → heart failure risk

slides.title: Signs and Symptoms
slides.subtitle: Hypertension is the "silent killer" — often asymptomatic until organ damage

blocks.heading: Early / Mild HTN
blocks.html:
• Headaches (esp. morning)
  • Dizziness / lightheadedness
  • Blurred vision
  • Epistaxis (nosebleeds)
  • Tinnitus (ringing in ears)
  • Often: no symptoms at all

blocks.heading: Severe HTN
blocks.html:
• Chest pain / dyspnea
  • Severe headache
  • Confusion / altered LOC
  • Hematuria
  • S4 gallop on auscultation
  • Displaced PMI

blocks.heading: HTN Crisis (BP >180/120)
blocks.html:
• Altered level of consciousness
  • Pulmonary edema
  • Acute kidney injury
  • Papilledema (on fundoscopy)
  • This is a medical emergency

Assess for organ damage NOW

blocks.heading: 👁 Fundoscopic Changes (HTN Severity)
blocks.html:
• Grade 1: Arteriolar narrowing
  • Grade 2: Arteriolar narrowing + AV nicking
  • Grade 3: Above + cotton-wool spots, hemorrhages
  • Grade 4: Above + papilledema (malignant HTN)

Retinal changes indicate HTN duration and severity

blocks.heading: 🔨 Link Patho to S/S
blocks.html:
Vessel damage → Headache, vision changes

LV strain → Chest pain, S4 gallop

Fluid overload → Dyspnea, edema

Renal damage → Hematuria, elevated Cr

Cerebral edema → Confusion, seizures
NRG Rule: S/S reflect pathophysiology. Ask: "What body system is affected? What is the priority?"

blocks.heading: Cardiovascular
blocks.html:
• BP in both arms (5 min rest)
  • Proper cuff size
  • Apical pulse, heart sounds
  • Check for edema, JVD

blocks.heading: Respiratory
blocks.html:
• Lung sounds (crackles = fluid)
  • Respiratory rate
  • SpO₂, dyspnea
  • Work of breathing

blocks.heading: Neurological
blocks.html:
• Level of consciousness
  • Headache severity
  • Visual changes
  • Speech assessment
🔬 Laboratory & Diagnostic Tests

NRG Priority: Accurate BP technique → 5 min rest, seated, arm at heart level, correct cuff size. Then assess all affected body systems.

Fundoscopy: Retinal changes indicate HTN severity. Always check in severe/long-standing HTN.
💊 Antihypertensives — Nursing Monitoring

blocks.heading: Beta-Blocker Alert: Metoprolol
blocks.html: Always check apical pulse before giving. Hold if HR <60 bpm. Also hold if SBP <90 mmHg. Monitor for bradycardia, hypotension, fatigue.

blocks.heading: DASH Diet & Lifestyle
blocks.html: Low sodium (<2g/day), high K⁺/Mg⁺, fruits/vegetables. Weight loss, regular exercise, smoking cessation, limit alcohol. Teach medication adherence.

blocks.heading: 🚨 Report Immediately
blocks.html:
BP >180/120 mmHg • Severe headache • Chest pain • Vision changes • Dyspnea • Altered LOC • Decreased urine output

NRG Safety Rule: All medications as prescribed • Monitor therapeutic and adverse effects • Document all findings

blocks.heading: Nursing Diagnosis
blocks.html: Ineffective tissue perfusion (cardiopulmonary) related to increased vascular resistance as evidenced by BP 160/100 mmHg, headache, dizziness

blocks.heading: Goal / Outcome
blocks.html: BP will decrease to <140/90 mmHg within 24 hours of medication administration. Patient will verbalize 3 lifestyle modifications.

blocks.heading: Interventions
blocks.html:
• Administer prescribed antihypertensives
  • Monitor BP q4h
  • Teach DASH diet principles
  • Encourage weight loss & exercise
  • Assess medication adherence

blocks.heading: Rationale
blocks.html:
Reducing vascular resistance and blood volume decreases cardiac workload and prevents end-organ damage. Lifestyle modifications address root causes of HTN.

Evaluation: BP 138/86. Patient verbalizes understanding of DASH diet and medication regimen. Follow-up scheduled.
NRG Care Plan Formula: Problem related to cause as evidenced by S/S → Goal → Interventions → Rationale → Evaluation

blocks.heading: What system is being tested?
blocks.html: Cardiovascular — BP regulation and tissue perfusion

blocks.heading: What is the priority?
blocks.html: Accurate BP assessment + meds + lifestyle teaching

blocks.heading: What is unsafe?
blocks.html: Giving antihypertensives without checking BP; not holding beta-blockers when HR <60

blocks.heading: What restores function?
blocks.html: Vasodilation + reduced volume = lower BP + improved perfusion

blocks.heading: 💡 Key Memory Aids for RENR
blocks.html:
HTN Crisis: BP >180/120 = assess for organ damage (neuro, cardiac, renal, vision)

ACE Inhibitors: "ACE inhibitors cause the ACE cough" + hyperkalemia + angioedema

Thiazide Diuretics: "hypoK" (hypokalemia) + hyperglycemia + hyperuricemia

Beta-Blockers: Always check apical pulse before giving

African Caribbean patients: CCBs and thiazides are first-line

JNC 8: <150/90 (age >60) or <140/90 (age <60 + diabetes/CKD)
NRG System Focus Formula: HTN → Cardiovascular → Vessel resistance → End-organ damage risk → Priority: BP control + organ protection

question.stem: A patient with hypertension is prescribed lisinopril. The nurse should monitor for which potential adverse effect?
question.rationale:
ACE inhibitors like lisinopril block angiotensin-converting enzyme, which can cause a dry, nonproductive cough in 5-20% of patients. This is a class effect. If the cough becomes intolerable, the patient may be switched to an ARB.

Why the others are wrong:

A. Peripheral edema = calcium channel blocker side effect

C. Bradycardia = beta-blocker side effect (check pulse before giving)

D. Hypokalemia = thiazide diuretic side effect; ACE inhibitors cause hyperkalemia
